Commitment: Lower inflation and grow the economy to ease the cost of living and create better paying jobs.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Stats NZ (17/09/2026) reported GDP up 0.2% in the June 2026 quarter (March revised to 0.9%); annual GDP up 1.7% but GDP per capita only 0.1% and real gross national disposable income down 0.4%. June quarter CPI took annual inflation to 4.1%, the highest since Dec 2023 and above the RBNZ 1-3% band, driven by fuel prices from the Middle East conflict; core measures about 2.5-3.0%. September quarter CPI is due shortly (Westpac forecasts 3.7%). Growth positive but inflation outside target, so held at 20.

Commitment: Let Kiwis keep more of what they earn with tax relief of up to $100 per fortnight for an average income household and a FamilyBoost childcare tax credit of up to $150 per fortnight.
Build infrastructure with 13 new Roads of National Significant and four major public transport upgrades.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 30/07/2026 the Crown signed the $3.6b Warkworth to Te Hana PPP (Northland Expressway Stage 1) with Northway; early works due within months, main construction from Nov 2027, opening about 2033. NZTA Major Transport Projects Pipeline (09/07/2026) put five RoNS in the slow lane with no construction timeline (incl. East-West Link, Petone to Grenada, Hope Bypass Stage 2). Ō2NL, Hawke's Bay Expressway, Takitimu North Link Stage 1 and SH29 Tauriko West under construction; Cambridge to Piarere funded in Budget 2026. Not near full delivery of 13 RoNS plus 4 PT upgrades.

Commitment: Restore law and order by backing Police to tackle gangs, boot camps for serious young offenders, and stronger sentencing so New Zealanders can feel safe
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill, creating Youth Court military-style academy orders, passed third reading under urgency on 17/09/2026; Royal Assent and commencement not yet confirmed. Second voluntary military-style academy cohort ran from Mar 2026 (pilot had high reoffending). Gang patch ban and dispersal laws in force; Three Strikes restored. Government reports violent crime reduction target tracking ahead.

Commitment: Lift school achievement by teaching kids an hour each of reading, writing and maths every day, banning cell phone use at school, and regular assessment and reporting to parents.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: From Term 1 2026, a national reporting framework gives parents of Years 0-10 standardised reports on reading, writing and maths progress (five descriptors), with twice-yearly progress check-ins for Years 3-8 using specified tools (1News, 02/02/2026). Cellphone ban in force from Term 2 2024; hour a day of reading, writing and maths required from 2024.

Commitment: Cut health waiting times by training more doctors, nurses, and midwives, and giving Kiwis access to 13 more cancer treatments.
Support seniors by maintaining the Winter Energy Payment, increasing Super every year and boosting it with our tax relief plan, which will see a superannuitant couple get over $600 extra each year.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: All three limbs met. NZ Super rose on 1 April each year of the term, most recently 01/04/2026 (Annual General Adjustment, wage growth 2.91%). Winter Energy Payment kept and paid 1 May to 1 October 2026. Income tax relief in force from 31/07/2024. Calls from researchers and the Greens to replace the WEP with a solar subsidy have not been adopted.

Commitment: Deliver Net Zero by 2050 including by doubling New Zealand’s renewable electricity and supporting new technology to reduce agricultural emissions.
Notes: Dec 2024: Second Emissions Reduction Plan released. Aug 2024: Electrify NZ plan with RMA reforms for renewables. Dec 2025: Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill introduced. $2bn BlackRock fund for 100% renewable electricity. More renewable generation commissioned in past 18 months than 15 years. BUT: Government axed Clean Car Discount, weakened methane pricing, and ETS reform; ag emissions policy ambiguous.

Commitment: Tax relief will be progressed as set out in National’s Tax Plan, but will not include a repeal of the foreign buyer’s residential property ban, with income tax reductions coming into force from 1 July 2024
Reduce Core Crown expenditure as a proportion of the overall economy.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Financial Statements of the Government for the year ended 30/06/2026 (released 08/10/2026) show core Crown expenses at 32.0% of GDP, down from 32.5% in 2024/25 and 33.0% in 2023/24, though above the 31.7% of 2022/23. Fiscal Strategy Report 2026 aims to reduce core Crown expenses towards 30% of GDP over time.

Commitment: Establish a select committee inquiry into banking competition with broad and deep criteria to focus on competitiveness, customer services, and profitability.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Finance and Expenditure Committee inquiry into banking competition was under way by 16/08/2024, taking submissions on terms covering competition, pricing, profitability, barriers to entry, regulation and rural lending. The Finance Minister had requested it on 12–13/06/2024. The committee reported in August 2025 and the Government agreed or partly agreed to all 19 recommendations in November 2025 (dates from news reporting, not checked against primary records).

Commitment: Explore options to strengthen the powers of the Grocery Commissioner, to improve competitiveness, and to address the lack of a third entrant to remove the market power of a duopoly
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: ComCom's grocery report (02/06/2026) found little change: the major retailers still hold 82% of the market. MBIE published the Cabinet paper 'Next steps for improving retail grocery competition' on 15/04/2026, following 2025 work on a request for information to potential entrants and divestment cost-benefit advice. The Government did not take a break-up to Cabinet this term; in September 2026 National campaigned on a Foodstuffs split. No change to the Grocery Commissioner's powers was found, and no third entrant has arrived.

Commitment: Assess and respond to the impact that energy prices have on inflation including consumer led institutional improvements.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Since 01/07/2026, Electricity Authority rules have required retailers with more than 5% market share to offer time-of-use plans and fairer solar export prices. These came out of the 2025 Energy Competition Task Force. Electricity prices were still up 12% a year in the June 2026 CPI, so the effect on inflation is unresolved. No broader institutional reform of the electricity market was found.

Commitment: By or before 2026, assess the impact inflation has had on the average tax rates faced by income earners.
Notes: Treasury Analytical Note AN 25/07 (Oct 2025) explicitly assesses fiscal drag: from 2011 to 2023 it lifted personal tax revenue by 1.6% of GDP and will increasingly hit lower-income earners if thresholds stay frozen. The July 2024 threshold lift was a partial response; Budget 2026 left PAYE bands unchanged, so average tax rates are rising again.

Commitment: As an export dependent nation, prioritise free and fair trade agreements, including with India
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: MFAT confirms the NZ-India FTA was signed in New Delhi on 27/04/2026; both countries completed ratification on 21/09/2026 and it is scheduled to enter into force on 20/10/2026. Coalition parties publicly disagreed over the deal; Labour backed it. NZ has also signed FTAs with the UAE, UK and EU during the term.

Commitment: The Coalition Government will increase funding for IRD tax audits to urgently expand the IRD tax audit capacity, minimise taxation losses due to insufficient IRD oversight, and to ensure greater integrity and fairness in our tax system
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered with changes. IRD compliance funding rose in three Budgets: $29m a year (Budget 2024, from July 2024), $35m a year (Budget 2025) and about $15m a year (Budget 2026, 28/05/2026), with revenue targets of $1.23bn then $1.33bn. Compromise: IRD has not ring-fenced extra audit staff, so expanded audit capacity is shown by revenue collected rather than audit headcount.

Commitment: Strengthen obligations on Jobseeker work ready beneficiaries to find work and make use of sanctions for non-compliance with work obligations, and consider time limits for under 25s.
Commit to moderate increases to the minimum wage every year.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The adult minimum wage rose every year of the term: $23.15 (01/04/2024), $23.50 (01/04/2025) and $23.95 (01/04/2026, announced by MBIE on 12/12/2025). These are moderate rises of roughly 1.5–2%, which critics said were below inflation. All annual reviews in this term delivered an increase.

Commitment: Improve the Accredited Employer Work Visa to focus the immigration system on attracting the workers and skills New Zealand needs.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: From 01/06/2026, AEWV applicants in skill level 3 roles must show English at IELTS 4.0 or equivalent (INZ announcement, 25/05/2026). This follows the 2025 AEWV changes and tougher rules for employers who favour migrants over local workers. Reform is substantial but ongoing; no AEWV change after June 2026 was found.

Commitment: Ensure Immigration New Zealand is engaged in proper risk management and verification to ensure migrants are filling genuine workforce needs.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Immigration (Enhanced Risk Management) Amendment Bill (introduced 18/03/2026) was reported back by the Education and Workforce Committee on 07/08/2026, recommending it pass. It strengthens compliance and enforcement, information-gathering and verification powers. No second or third reading was confirmed. Exploitation prosecutions continue, so operational verification of genuine workforce need is still incomplete.

Commitment: Investigate the establishment of an “Essential Worker” workforce planning mechanism to better plan for skill or labour shortages in the long term.
Commit to enforcement and action to ensure those found responsible for the abuse of migrant workers face appropriate consequences.
Notes: Jun 2026: Budget 2026 sets aside $18m over 4 years for migrant exploitation enforcement. Jul 2025: Bill criminalising migrant exploitation (up to 7 years jail, $100k fines). Apr 2024: INZ infringement penalties in effect. Multiple successful prosecutions: Kiwifruit boss $40k, Thai massage $200k+, dairy farmer $200k. On 7 August 2026 the Enhanced Risk Management Bill was reported back; it would lift the maximum sentence for migrant exploitation (and for charging employment premiums) from 7 to 10 years. Budget 2026’s $18m / 22 extra frontline staff remain the operational backbone. Not yet enacted.

Commitment: Address and provide solutions for the long-expressed concern of the OECD into the lack of focus in New Zealand Immigration Policy
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Skilled Migrant Category changes took effect 24/08/2026 (new Skilled Work Experience and Trades and Technician pathways, simplified median-wage settings, NZ-qualification points), following earlier AEWV, English-language and parent visa changes. The May 2024 OECD survey flagged immigration settings; the reset is broad but no response framed against the OECD critique was found. Commitment wording is vague; 20 reflects partial progress.

Commitment: Establish a National Infrastructure Agency
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The National Infrastructure Agency was established by repurposing Crown Infrastructure Partners and began operating on 1 December 2024 as National Infrastructure Funding and Financing Ltd (Treasury; Te Waihanga notice 2 Dec 2024). It is the Crown's shopfront for infrastructure investors and administers infrastructure funds. Announced by Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop on 28 Aug 2024. The 30-year National Infrastructure Plan and new ministry are related but separate.

Commitment: Prioritise strategic infrastructure to improve the resilience of heavy industry in New Zealand.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Feb 2026: Government decided to contract an LNG import facility to protect energy security for gas-dependent industry; June 2026 update shortlisted two Port Taranaki providers, possibly operating by 2028, levy funding dropped. No contract signed found. May 2026: NZ First campaign proposal for a Special Economic Zone at Marsden Point (party policy, not government action). No dedicated heavy-industry resilience programme delivered.

Commitment: Establish a Regional Infrastructure Fund with $1.2 billion in capital funding over the Parliamentary term.
Repeal the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023 and the Spatial Planning Act 2023.
Amend the Resource Management Act 1991
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Planning Act 2026 and Natural Environment Act 2026 received Royal Assent and came into force on 30 Sep 2026, replacing the RMA framework; transitional arrangements begin about 30 Oct 2026 and an amended RMA continues during a multi-year transition until repealed by Order in Council. Planning Tribunal due 2027. Earlier RMA amendment Acts (2024–25) were already in force. No primary legislation.govt.nz record could be fetched; source is law-firm commentary.

Commitment: Cancel Auckland Light Rail
Cancel Let's Get Wellington Moving
Reduce expenditure on cycleways
Commit to building a four-lane highway alternative for the Brynderwyns and investigate the use of private finance to accelerate construction.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Crown signed a PPP with the Northway consortium for Northland Expressway Stage 1 (Warkworth–Te Hana), reported 30/07/2026: $3.65bn NPV, opening 2033. That delivers the private-finance investigation for the corridor. NZTA lodged Fast-track route-protection and consent applications for the 17km Brynderwyn Hills alternative (Kaiwaka–Waipū) in May 2026, after the route was announced in April 2025. The Brynderwyns section has no construction contract or funding yet.

Commitment: Investigate the threshold at which local lines companies can invest in generation assets.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The 9/06/2026 Government Policy Statement to the Electricity Authority says the Government 'is considering the thresholds' for distributor investment in generation. MBIE's investigation of amending or removing the caps (50 MW on own network, 250 MW grid-connected) was proactively released in 2025, after ministers said on 27/02/2025 the restrictions would be eased through an Energy and Electricity Security Bill. No law change found in force.

Commitment: Commission a study into New Zealand’s fuel security requirements.
Facilitate the development and efficiency of ports and strengthen international supply networks.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Port of Tauranga's $1bn+ Stella Passage expansion was approved under the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 (reported 07/09/2026; subject to appeal). The RM (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Act 2025 extended s384A port coastal permits to 30/09/2046, citing this commitment, and the $30m Coastal Shipping Resilience Fund has funded port and shipping projects. No national ports or supply-chain strategy found; facilitation is ongoing.

Commitment: Commence an urgent review into the implementation of the National Policy Statement on Indigenous Biodiversity before any implementation.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The NPSIB Amendment 2025 (gazetted 18/12/2025, in force 15/01/2026) changed consent pathways for quarrying and mining after the 2025 national direction review. New SNA identification was suspended for 3 years by the October 2024 RMA amendment to allow the review. The review started before implementation, but no full replacement of the NPSIB has been made.

Commitment: Replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 and the National Environmental Standards for Freshwater to better reflect the interests of all water users.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The NPS-FM 2020 Amendment 2025 (gazetted 18/12/2025, in force 15/01/2026) added 'operational need' for quarrying and mining. Options to replace the NPS-FM and rebalance Te Mana o te Wai were consulted on May–July 2025, but no replacement NPS-FM or NES-F has been gazetted. Due date 20/12/2024 has passed.

Commitment: Investigate the reopening of Marsden Point Refinery. This includes establishing a Fuel Security Plan to safeguard our transport and logistics systems and emergency services from any international or domestic disruption.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: MBIE published the Fuel Security Plan on 05/11/2025 (extra diesel stockholding from July 2028, jet-fuel resilience at Auckland Airport, alternative fuels). It was informed by the Envisory/Castalia Fuel Security Study, which included a report on re-establishing the Marsden Point refinery (interim estimate NZ$4.9–7.3bn). The Government chose a strategic diesel reserve at Marsden Point (operational July 2026) rather than reopening the refinery.

Commitment: Progress further work examining connecting the railway to Marsden Point and Northport from the Northern Main Truck Line.
Notes: 2 Jun 2026: KiwiRail design sprint with Acciona, Downer/HEB, Martinus to lower cost before funding decision. Progress beyond investigate; construction funding not committed.

Commitment: Progress the detailed business case for a dry dock at Marsden Point to service domestic and international shipping needs and to support our Navy vessels, with investigation of funding options including commercial partnerships.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: MBIE, delivering the Northland shipyard and dry dock for the Crown with Northport's technical support, lodged a Fast-track consent application with the EPA on 20/08/2026. Cabinet (May 2025) agreed up to $100m from the Regional Infrastructure Fund and sought an updated detailed business case (including a longer dock option) before final investment decisions. The March 2025 Investment Summit sought commercial partners. The final business case and investment decision are not yet public.

Commitment: Require the electricity regulator to implement regulations such that there is sufficient electricity infrastructure to ensure security of supply and avoid excessive prices.
Notes: Transpower was given additional powers to manage electricity supply risks in March 2025 as the sector sought to avoid a repeat of the prior year's shortages. 9 Jun 2026 GPS to the Electricity Authority (s17 Electricity Industry Act) directs the regulator to serve consumers 'through the provision of sufficient electricity infrastructure to ensure security of supply and avoid excessive prices'. Oct 2025 Energy Package added EA monitoring and Transpower risk-assessment roles; further legislation was flagged for 2026.

Commitment: Examine transmission and connection pricing to facilitate cost effective connection of new renewable generation resources, both on-shore and off-shore.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Electricity Authority opened consultation on further distribution connection-pricing reform on 13 Jul 2026 (cross-submissions closed 17 Sep 2026), after deciding on 1 Jul 2026 new rules targeting high up-front connection charges; first fast-track rules took effect 1 Apr 2026. Transmission pricing (TPM) changes are a separate workstream. No completed examination of connection settings for offshore generation found.

Commitment: Plan for transitional low carbon fuels, including the infrastructure needed to increase the use of methanol and hydrogen to achieve sovereign fuel resilience.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 12 Aug 2026 $30m Regional Infrastructure Fund hydrogen package; in-principle Cabinet decisions on natural/orange hydrogen regulation still pending. Fuel Security Plan (Nov 2025) supports domestic low-carbon fuels and a renewable-diesel standard; Hydrogen Action Plan Nov 2024. On 2 Sep 2026 Methanex said it will idle its NZ methanol plants from early 2027 after selling its gas, undercutting the methanol limb. LNG import terminal work is adjacent rather than the named fuels.

Commitment: Future-proof the natural gas industry by restarting offshore exploration and supporting development of hydrogen technology to produce hydrogen from natural gas without co-production of CO2.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: On 29 Jul 2026 NZ Petroleum and Minerals granted EnZed Energy a 12-year offshore exploration permit (about 546 km² east of the Kupe field, Taranaki Basin), the first new offshore permit since the ban was reversed; further applications are pending. Exploration limb substantially delivered. Hydrogen limb: only general hydrogen support (Hydrogen Action Plan, RIF funding); no specific programme for producing hydrogen from natural gas without CO2 found.

Commitment: Ensure that climate change policies are aligned and do not undermine national energy security.
Notes: Jun 2026 electricity GPS and the Oct 2025 Energy Package treat security of supply and thermal backup (including a proposed LNG terminal) as constraints on climate/electrification policy. ERP2 and the Hydrogen Action Plan similarly frame decarbonisation as subject to energy security. Alignment is a standing policy stance, not a finished project.

Commitment: Ensure the government’s energy settings allow for the exploration of natural geological hydrogen in New Zealand, to maximise future energy resilience.
Notes: May 2025 MBIE consultation on regulating natural (white) and orange hydrogen under the Crown Minerals Act or alternatives. On 12 Aug 2026 Shane Jones said he will seek in-principle Cabinet decisions shortly, with legislative change after the election. Exploration settings are not yet amended.

Commitment: Investigate the strategic opportunities in New Zealand’s mineral resources, including vanadium, and develop a plan to develop these opportunities.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 6 Jul 2026 Govt offered up to $50m from the Regional Infrastructure Fund to Tāiko Critical Minerals (Barrytown) and Westland Mineral Sands (Westport) processing plants, conditional on private capital. The Critical Minerals List (vanadium included) and Minerals Strategy aim to double mineral exports by 2035. The main vanadium prospect, Trans-Tasman Resources' South Taranaki seabed mine, was withdrawn from fast-track in Feb 2026 after a draft decline.

Commitment: Stop the current review of the ETS system to restore confidence and certainty to the carbon trading market.
Notes: Government exempted farmers from ETS pricing in June 2024 and set up a new working group, effectively halting the prior He Waka Eke Noa pricing workstream. 6 Dec 2023: Government announced it had immediately stopped the previous Labour Government's NZ ETS review. MfE's consultation page confirms 'Work on the ETS review has now ceased' (results updated 25 Mar 2025). Later ETS settings/forestry changes are separate from stopping that review.

Commitment: Progress work to recognise other forms of carbon sequestration, including blue carbon.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: MfE is accepting applications for science assessments of non-forestry carbon removal activities under the Assessment Framework for Carbon Removals (applicant guide May 2026; opening date unconfirmed). The framework was released 04/11/2025, alongside proposals to let other removals into the NZ ETS later. Wetlands and peatlands identified as opportunities; no blue-carbon activity yet recognised in the ETS.

Commitment: Incentivise the uptake of emissions reduction mitigations, such as low methane genetics, and low methane producing animal feed.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 29 Apr 2026 AgriZeroNZ, MPI, Beef + Lamb NZ and the Ag Emissions Centre committed $1.2m to extend the Cool Sheep programme, improving methane breeding values to encourage uptake of low-methane sheep genetics. Government also co-funds mitigation R&D through AgriZeroNZ. No comprehensive incentive scheme for low-methane genetics or feed is in force. Q4 2024 due date has passed.

Commitment: Support Farm Environment Plans administered by regional councils and targeted at a catchment level.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 19/08/2026 Cabinet decisions (Natural Environment Bill amendment paper; regulations still to be drafted) make freshwater farm plans risk-based: certification/audit only for higher-risk activities, other farms declare plans to councils, five years from switch-on, council catchment context clarified. Builds on Aug 2025 changes (pastoral/arable threshold raised to 50 ha, ~8,000 farms exempt). Rollout paused since Oct 2024 except Southland. Council-administered, catchment-based model retained but simplified.

Commitment: Adopt standardised farm level reporting.
Notes: 13 Dec 2024: Government released a standardised, science-based farm-level GHG measurement methodology (MPI) as its Q4 commitment, aligning calculators on farm-specific inputs. Mandatory universal farm-level reporting does not appear to have been imposed.

Commitment: Cut red tape and regulatory blocks on irrigation, water storage, managed aquifer recharge and flood protection schemes.
Notes: May 2025 freshwater national-direction consultation explicitly proposed 'removing regulatory blocks for creating water storage' and enabling irrigation-related activities around wetlands. Some water-storage projects are on the fast-track list. Replacement NPS-FM/NES-F instruments that would cut those blocks have not been gazetted; IrrigationNZ still argued in Feb 2026 that water infrastructure is missing from RM reform.

Commitment: Amend the National Environmental Standards for Plantation Forestry (NES-PF) regulations to place a duty upon harvesters to contain and remove post-harvest slash.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: NES-CF amendments in force 04/06/2026 replace the 2023 fixed slash size/volume removal rules (regs 69(5)-(7)) with a Slash Mobilisation Risk Assessment for orange/red-zone harvests; low-risk sites manage slash via harvest plan conditions, higher-risk sites need consent. A harvester duty to assess and manage slash exists, but the blanket removal requirement was softened rather than strengthened. Partial delivery.

Commitment: Direct government agencies where practical and appropriate to preference the use of woollen fibres rather than artificial fibres in government buildings.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: From 01/07/2025 about 130 agencies under the Government Procurement Rules are directed (Construction Procurement Guide under Rule 69) to use woollen fibres where practical and appropriate in new builds of $9m+ and refurbishments of $100k+, documenting and reporting annually to MBIE when not. Announced 09/04/2025; MBIE Cabinet paper titled 'Fulfilling the coalition commitment'. Kāinga Ora moved to wool carpet in new homes from 01/07/2025.

Commitment: Reverse the recent ban on live animal exports while ensuring the highest standards of animal welfare.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 10/03/2026 Associate Agriculture Minister Andrew Hoggard said Cabinet would not agree to reinstate live export by sea, so reversing the ban will not progress this term despite a promise to have legislation in Parliament. The ban (Labour, 2023) remains in place; the term ends with the 2026 election.

Commitment: Reform the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee to ensure its functions, membership and mandate are appropriate.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: NAWAC's 2025 annual report (approved April 2026) says its code-of-conduct guideline remains on hold awaiting 'proposed reform of NAWAC's function, membership and mandate', so the reform is not done. June 2024 ministerial expectations letter directed NAWAC to weigh practicality and cost, engage stakeholders and reprioritise codes (a 'first step'). The Oct 2025 pig-code override is not a reform of NAWAC.

Commitment: Deliver longer durations for marine farming permits and remove regulations that impede the productivity and enormous potential of the seafood sector.
Notes: Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Act 2024 received Royal Assent 2 Sep 2024, automatically extending existing marine-farm coastal permits by 20 years (capped at 31 Dec 2050). NES for Marine Aquaculture amendments (announced May 2026, in force 4 Jun 2026) ease reconsenting and on-farm changes. Broader seafood-sector deregulation remains incomplete.

Commitment: Liberalise genetic engineering laws while ensuring strong protections for human health and the environment.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Gene Technology Bill introduced and first read 17/12/2024; Health Committee reported back 10/10/2025 recommending passage by majority. NZ First lodged a differing view and will not support it without major changes; on 14/06/2026 Peters said it would not be put forward this term. An advocacy release (23/07/2026) reported a second reading was scheduled, but no vote was confirmed. Not enacted.

Commitment: Commit to training no fewer than 500 new frontline police within the first two years.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Failed. The two-year deadline passed on 27/11/2025 with the target officially missed: 10,449 constable FTEs at 17/11/2025 against a 10,211 baseline (target 10,711). Treasury projected the 500 would be reached in September 2026, but the commitment was time-bound to the first two years. Recruitment is still funded and continuing.

Commitment: Increase the number of the trained Youth Aid Officers over the term.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Budget 2024 (30/05/2024) funded an extra 500 police officers ($226.1m), and the Government's 'Backing the Police' factsheet says they will be used partly to increase the number of Youth Aid Officers. No published Youth Aid headcount found (Police reports, OIA requests on fyi.org.nz and written questions all searched), so whether numbers have actually risen is unverified.

Commitment: Adequately resource community policing, including Māori and Pasifika wardens, Community Patrol New Zealand, and Neighbourhood Watch.
Notes: First public action: community police teams announced in major cities (June 2024); national gang unit established (May 2024). No specific ringfenced funding boost for Māori/Pasifika wardens, Community Patrol NZ or Neighbourhood Watch found. Budget 2025 put $1.5m a year of new baseline funding into Māori Wardens (Beehive 17 May 2025). Budget 2026 added further funding for Pasifika Wardens, Neighbourhood Support NZ and Community Patrols NZ (National/Mitchell 28 May 2026). Named groups now have ringfenced boosts; whether the resource is 'adequate' is still unverified.

Commitment: Introduce a suite of measures designed to tackle youth crime including consideration of a Youth Justice Demerit Point system.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered with changes. Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Act 2026 in force 26/09/2026, creating young serious offender declarations and Youth Court military-style academy orders. MSA pilot ran Jul 2024 to Jul 2025; a second programme began 09/03/2026. Compromise: no record was found that a Youth Justice Demerit Point system was formally considered. Labour says it would repeal the Act.

Commitment: Reform the Fleeing Driver laws to curb the increase in fleeing driver incidents.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Antisocial Road Use Legislation Amendment Act 2026 received Royal Assent 9 Jul 2026 (passed 30 Jun 2026) but comes into force on 9 Jan 2027 (s 2). It adds presumptive vehicle forfeiture or destruction for drivers who flee Police and street racers, Police powers to close roads at antisocial gatherings, and higher noise infringement fees. Enacted, not yet in force; 100 once it commences.

Commitment: Amend the Sentencing Act 2002 and associated legislation to ensure appropriate consequences for criminals, including: Giving priority to the needs of victims and communities over offenders. Including gang membership as an aggravating factor during sentencing. Including the victim working sole charge or adjacent to a dwelling as an aggravating factor during sentencing. Ensuring real consequences for lower-level crimes such as shoplifting. Removing concurrent sentences for those who commit offences while on parole, on bail, or whilst in custody.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Crimes Amendment Act 2026 in force 8 Aug 2026, adding a theft in an offensive or disorderly manner offence; its retail-theft infringement notice regime (ss 35–39) commences by Order in Council or on 7 Feb 2027 at the latest. Earlier: gang membership as an aggravating factor (2024), three strikes reinstated (Dec 2024), and the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act 2025 (sole-charge/home aggravating factors, victim-priority discount caps, concurrent sentences for offending on bail, parole or in custody). Held at 90 until the shoplifting infringement limb is in force.

Commitment: Where appropriate, require prisoners to work, including in the construction of new accommodation in prisons or pest control.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: No coalition-era policy, funding or law change found that requires or expands prisoner work, or puts prisoners on prison construction or pest control. Corrections Act 2004 s 66 already lets prison managers direct sentenced prisoners to work (no change this term), and prison industries and Release to Work predate the commitment. The youth boot camp pilot is not prisoner work.

Commitment: Equip corrections officers with body cameras and protective equipment, where appropriate.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Corrections officers are already equipped with stab-resistant body armour, body-worn cameras and pepper spray (Corrections Minister, RNZ 17/08/2025; NZ Herald 13/02/2026). The Police Association reports 2,500 Axon cameras issued to prison officers since 2021. This equipment predates the coalition and continues, and no new coalition-era rollout was found.

Commitment: Seek to make it easier for New Zealanders, including prisoners, to get drivers licences, and better support to existing programmes that are delivering positive outcomes.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Government confirmed 3 Feb 2026 that the second practical test for a full car licence will be scrapped and costs cut by $80 from 25 Jan 2027, though under-25s get a longer learner period. No new support for prisoner licensing or existing programmes (e.g. the Corrections-funded Howard League driving programme) found. Whangārei unlicensed-driving court (Aug 2024) is adjacent.

Commitment: Introduce the Protection for First Responders and Prison Officers legislation which will create a specific offence for assaults on first responders which includes minimum mandatory prison sentences.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered with changes. Crimes Amendment Act 2026 in force 08/08/2026, creating specific offences for assaulting or injuring first responders and front-line corrections workers (up to 3, 5 and 7 years). Change: no mandatory minimum sentences were included; injuring with intent is a Three Strikes offence instead. NZ First criticised the omission.

Commitment: Introduce the Coward Punch legislation which will create a specific offence for anyone who injures or kills someone with a coward punch.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Crimes Amendment Act 2026 (assent 7 Aug 2026) in force 8 Aug 2026. New s 171A (manslaughter by strike to head or neck, up to life) and s 188A (wounding with intent by strike to head or neck: 15 years if GBH intended, 8 years if intent to injure or reckless). NZ First called the law 'window dressing' (12 Jun 2026) but the specific coward-punch offences are in force.

Commitment: Investigate the introduction and implementation of Degrees of Murder Sentencing legislation.
Enforce compulsory education and address truancy.
Refocus the curriculum on academic achievement and not ideology, including the removal and replacement of the gender, sexuality, and relationship-based education guidelines.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Final Years 0-10 curriculum completed 16/09/2026 with release of the Health and PE and Arts learning areas, giving a consistent national approach to sexuality education and replacing reliance on 2007 guidance; biennial community consultation requirement removed. Schools must implement by 2027 (Years 9-10) and 2029 (Years 0-8). The 2020 RSE guidelines were removed from the Ministry website in March 2025. Not 100 until the new curriculum is in use.

Commitment: Stop first year Fees Free and replace with a final year Fees Free with no change before 2025.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Peters disclosed and Finance Minister Willis confirmed on 08/05/2026 that final-year Fees Free will be scrapped; 2026 is the last year students qualify, and Budget 2026 (28/05/2026) confirmed it. First-year Fees Free had ended and the final-year scheme started on 1 January 2025 as committed. Partial delivery then walked back.

Commitment: Maintain the Apprenticeship Boost scheme.
Notes: No explicit announcement found maintaining or expanding Apprenticeship Boost under the coalition — implicit continuation through TEC contracts. Treat as low-confidence positive fraction. Apprenticeship Boost continued past prior sunset (Budget 2024 $64m) and retargeted to priority first-year apprentices from Jan 2025. Scheme maintained as committed.

Commitment: Abolish the Māori Health Authority.
Update Pharmac’s decision making model to ensure it appropriately takes “patient’s voice” into account and increase funding for Pharmac every year.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 04/08/2026: Seymour announced a Community and Patient Advisory Committee to replace the Consumer Advisory Committee and Consumer Working Group; recruitment from October 2026, committee expected in the New Year. Funding: $604m uplift (2024) and a $6.294b four-year budget. Patient Voice Aotearoa (April 2026) criticised slow decision-making. Formal decision-making model rewrite is not yet complete.

Commitment: Require Medsafe to approve new pharmaceuticals within 30 days of them being approved by at least two overseas regulatory agencies recognised by New Zealand.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered with changes. Medicines (Consent by Verification) Rules 2026 in force 03/07/2026, operating the Rule-of-Two pathway from the Medicines Amendment Act 2025; recognised regulators gazetted 16/02/2026. Compromise: the pathway is opt-in, triggered by a sponsor application, and the limit is 30 working days rather than 30 days. No approval under it found yet.

Commitment: Better recognise people with overseas medical qualifications and experience for accreditation in New Zealand.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 15/07/2025: Medical Council added Chile, Luxembourg and Croatia to the Comparable Health System pathway (29 countries, 20-working-day processing), launched a GP fast-track for US/Canada/Singapore and cut provisional vocational processing to 3 months. Specialist fast-track (UK/Ireland/Australia) from late 2024; Japan and South Korea added Feb 2025. No newer Medical Council change found in 2026.

Commitment: Progress the adoption of digital technology in harder to staff areas and make greater use of Nurse Practitioners.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 12/05/2026: Brown said 120 nurse practitioner training places are funded each year, and the Medicines Amendment Act lets NPs prescribe section 29 unapproved medicines. Digital: 24/7 Online GP Care launched nationally on 01/07/2025, giving virtual GP and nurse access from anywhere; Budget 2026 added $153.6m for Health NZ digital upgrades. No hard-to-staff-area digital programme or NP scope expansion beyond this found.

Commitment: Repeal the Therapeutic Products Act 2023.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Therapeutic Products Act Repeal Act 2024 received Royal assent on 17/12/2024 and commenced the next day; the Therapeutic Products Act 2023 was repealed on 18/12/2024 (s 3 of the Repeal Act). The Repeal Act itself expired on 14/01/2025.

Commitment: Fund Gumboot Friday/I Am Hope Charity to $6 million per annum.
Renegotiate the Crown funding agreement with St John with a view to meeting a greater portion of their annualised budget.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Budget 2026 (22/05/2026) gave Hato Hone St John $35m over four years for specific initiatives, including two Auckland ambulance hubs, but St John said baseline funding in the next four-year contract with ACC and Health NZ was still to be negotiated. No new agreement found since. Earlier: extra $21m in Oct 2024 lifted the 2024/25 Crown contribution to about $357m (roughly 82–83% of costs).

Commitment: Ensure Plunket is funded to do their job properly.
Ensure proper funding for birthing units and maternity care, including providing for a three day stay for new mothers.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) (3 Day Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill passed its final stage on 23/09/2026, the last sitting day before the election. Entitlement to up to 72 hours of inpatient postnatal care is phased in, first-time mothers first, with full national availability by 01/07/2029. Budget 2026 gave $34.4m over four years for maternity bed capacity and workforce. No separate birthing-unit funding identified.

Commitment: Repeal amendments to the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act 1990 and regulations before March 2024, removing requirements for denicotisation, removing the reduction in retail outlets and the generation ban, while also amending vaping product requirements and taxing smoked products only.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered with changes. The 2022 amendments (denicotisation, retail outlet reduction, generation ban) were repealed on 06/03/2024 by the Amendment Act 2024. The Amendment Act (No 2) 2024 (assent 17/12/2024) changed vaping product and retail rules, with the last provisions in force 17/06/2025. Change: tax was not limited to smoked products; heated tobacco excise was halved instead.

Commitment: Reform the regulation of vaping, smokeless tobacco and oral nicotine products while banning disposable vaping products and increasing penalties for illegal sales to those under 18.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Act (No 2) 2024 (assent 17/12/2024): higher fines for sales to under-18s ($100,000 / $10,000) in force 18/12/2024; disposable vape ban (s 20FA, fines up to $400,000) and tighter display and advertising rules in force 17/06/2025. Two of three limbs delivered; no comprehensive reform of smokeless tobacco and oral nicotine regulation found.

Commitment: Keep the superannuation age at 65.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Section 7 of the NZ Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001 (latest version) still sets eligibility at 65. National and ACT campaign to raise it to 67 (National from 2044), but no change was made this term; NZ First opposes any change.

Commitment: Amend the Building Act and the Resource Consent system to make it easier to build granny flats or other small structures up to 60sqm requiring only an engineer’s report.
Notes: Government announced policy to allow buildings up to 60sqm without resource consent in certain areas (5 Apr 2025). Building Act amendment progressing — partial delivery, engineer-only regime not yet finalised. Building and resource consent exemptions for granny flats up to 70m² took effect 15 Jan 2026 (Building Act + NES-DMRU). Commitment fully delivered.

Commitment: Progress the review of the Retirement Villages Act.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: On 03/12/2025 Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka announced changes to the Retirement Villages Act following MHUD's review: interest after 6 months if a unit is unsold, full repayment within 12 months, weekly fees stopping on exit, early access for need. A Retirement Villages Amendment Bill is referred to (RNZ, 23/06/2026) but its introduction could not be confirmed. Not enacted.

Commitment: Upgrade the Super Gold Card and Veterans Card to maximise its potential benefit for all Super Gold Card and Veteran Card holders.
Notes: Budget 2026 funds an optional SuperGold photo-ID upgrade ($36.4m operating and $6.46m capital). Cards expected from October 2028; existing cards remain valid.

Commitment: Investigate the funding formula for new residential care beds.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group report 'A place to grow old' was published August 2026 (released 17/08/2026). Its terms of reference covered the funding model needed for a sustainable supply of standard residential beds; it recommends differentiated accommodation funding to incentivise new rooms. Government response pending. Separately, $79m (~4%) ARC funding boost for 2026/27 announced 17/06/2026.

Commitment: Engage openly and constructively with the aged-care sector.
Notes: Government has engaged with the aged-care sector via a ministerial advisory group with sector 'liaison' on nominees, but no formal engagement framework has been published.

Commitment: Undertake a select committee inquiry into aged care provision to include supporting people with early onset conditions and what asset thresholds are appropriate in 2023/24.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Health Committee reported its inquiry into aged care capacity for people with neurological cognitive disorders to the House on 20/11/2025 (14 recommendations; Ministry papers give 21/11/2025 as publication date). The Government's response (March 2026) cites it as delivering this coalition commitment and refers its recommendations, including cost-sharing, to the Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group, which reported in August 2026.

Commitment: Explore options to build on the Local Government Rates Rebate Scheme for Super Gold Card holders.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Rates Rebate Amendment Act 2025 (assent 27/06/2025, in force 01/07/2025) gave SuperGold cardholders a separate income abatement threshold of $45,000 (other ratepayers $32,210), the first SuperGold-specific rates rebate setting. Thresholds are now indexed annually by Order in Council; for 2026/27 they are $46,400 for SuperGold cardholders and $33,210 for others. The exploration produced an enacted option, so the commitment is delivered.

Commitment: Work on establishing bipartisan agreement to fund both care and dementia beds that New Zealand needs now and with a focus on the long term needs by 2040.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Aged Care Ministerial Advisory Group (est. Dec 2025, chaired by former Labour health minister David Cunliffe, set up on a bipartisan basis per Cabinet Sept 2025) released its final report 'A place to grow old' in Aug 2026, recommending funding reform including larger uplifts for dementia-level beds, for 'any future government'. No cross-party funding agreement or 2040 bed target has been reached. Govt response to the Health Committee dementia inquiry (May 2026) defers to this work.

Commitment: Liaise with retirement village owners and occupiers to seek a mutually agreed way forward to safeguard the interests of the 50,000 plus New Zealanders living in retirement villages.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: On 04/12/2025 the Government announced Retirement Villages Act changes after a review that drew 11,000+ submissions: operators to repay former residents within 12 months (with interest after six months), to own chattels/fixture costs, and a new independent disputes scheme. An amendment bill was expected in 2026 but introduction is unverified. Residents' association says 12 months is too long; Labour backs a three-month members' bill.

Commitment: By December 1, 2023, lodge a reservation against adopting amendments to WHO health regulations to allow the government to consider these against a “national interest test”.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: On 29/11/2023 Cabinet reserved NZ's position on the 2022 IHR Article 59 amendments, ahead of the 01/12/2023 deadline, to allow a 'national interest test'; NZ keeps the former 24-month preparation and 18-month opt-out periods.

Commitment: Commit that in the absence of a referendum, our Government will not change the official name of New Zealand.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: No change to New Zealand's official name has been made or proposed by the Government; the name can only be changed by law. In March 2025 the Speaker ruled 'Aotearoa' may be used in the House as it is in common use, after Winston Peters argued any change needs a referendum. NZ First introduced a member's bill in Aug 2025 to enshrine 'New Zealand' as the official name. Met under the 'not change' wording since 27/11/2023.

Commitment: Support to select committee a bill that would enact a binding referendum on a four-year term of parliament.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered on the literal commitment. The four-year term bill had its first reading on 05/03/2025 and the Justice Committee reported back on 25/08/2025, completing the select committee stage. The bill has not progressed to second reading this term; that is outside this commitment. Moved from 20 to 100 on review (19/10/2026).

Commitment: Ensure publicly funded sporting bodies support fair competition that is not compromised by rules relating to gender.
Notes: Government ordered Sport NZ to scrap and remove trans-inclusive community sport guidelines in July 2025; IOC also brought in new gender eligibility rules in March 2026, aligning NZ policy direction.

Commitment: Legislate to make English an official language of New Zealand.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: English Language Act 2026 (2026 No 49) received Royal Assent on 6 August 2026 and came into force on 7 August 2026 (s 2). Section 5 states that English is an official language of New Zealand.

Commitment: Ensure all public service departments have their primary name in English, except for those specifically related to Māori.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 20 May 2026: at the direction of Public Service Minister Paul Goldsmith, the Public Service Commission told agencies to put 'New Zealand Government' in bold above 'Te Kāwanatanga o Aotearoa' on homepages by the end of June 2026, with physical materials to follow. RNZ does not report this as a change to department primary names; the 75 rests on earlier English-first naming not re-verified in this run.

Commitment: Require the public service departments and Crown Entities to communicate primarily in English - except those entities specifically related to Māori.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: PSC OIA response (12/08/2025) confirms no all-of-government 'communicate primarily in English' directive was issued; after Cabinet discussion in 2024 Minister Willis left it to individual ministers and agencies case by case. Some agencies changed practice (e.g. NZTA told to use English name first, Dec 2023), but there is no comprehensive requirement across departments and Crown entities.

Commitment: Protect freedom of speech by ruling out the introduction of hate speech legislation and stop the Law Commission’s work on hate speech legislation.
Notes: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith ordered the Law Commission to stop hate speech work in April 2024 and confirmed no new hate speech legislation will proceed; both halves of the commitment delivered.

Commitment: End all Covid-19 vaccine mandates still in operation.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: All government Covid-19 vaccine mandates ended in Sept 2022, before the coalition took office; in May 2024 Health Minister Reti conceded 'technically' all mandates had ended. Some employer workplace vaccination policies (e.g. Health NZ for high-risk staff) remain under health and safety rules; Reti said Cabinet would consider whether the pledge covers these, but no decision has been found.

Commitment: Ensure, as a matter of urgency in establishment and completion, a full scale, wide ranging, independent inquiry conducted publicly with local and international experts, into how the Covid pandemic was handled in New Zealand, including covering: use of multiple lockdowns, vaccine procurement and efficacy, the social and economic impacts on both regional and national levels, and whether the decisions made, and steps taken, where justified.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into COVID-19 Lessons Learned published its Phase Two reports on 10 March 2026, after delivering them to the Governor-General on 26 February 2026. Phase Two covered vaccine safety and mandates, testing procurement and the late-2021 lockdowns. The Inquiry is complete.

Commitment: Ensure a ‘National Interest Test’ is undertaken before New Zealand accepts any agreements from the UN and its agencies that limit national decision-making and reconfirm that New Zealand’s domestic law holds primacy over any international agreements.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: 16 May 2025: Peters and Brown said officials will run a full National Interest Test on the WHO Pandemic Agreement before any decision to sign. This is the first public use of a National Interest Test on a UN-agency instrument. There is no standing test for all such agreements, and the domestic-law-primacy limb has not been separately confirmed.

Commitment: The Coalition Government will defend the principle that New Zealanders are equal before the law, with the same rights and obligations, and with the guarantee of the privileges and responsibilities of equal citizenship in New Zealand.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Cabinet Office Circular CO (24) 5 'Needs-based Service Provision' (13/09/2024) requires public services to be targeted on need, not race, giving effect to coalition commitments; a PSC OIA response (04/05/2026) lists the supporting advice. No dedicated 'equal before the law' legislation or wider programme has followed, so this is an initial step only.

Commitment: The Coalition Government will work to improve outcomes for all New Zealanders, and will not advance policies that seek to ascribe different rights and responsibilities to New Zealanders on the basis of their race or ancestry.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Cabinet Office circular CO (24) 5 'Needs-based Service Provision' (13/09/2024) directs agencies to target, commission and design public services on need, giving effect to the coalition commitment. Broader race-based rights reform via the Treaty Principles Bill was defeated in April 2025; the separate Treaty clauses review continues. Held at 20 as a first-step directive.

Commitment: The Coalition Government will honour the undertakings made by the Crown through past Treaty of Waitangi settlements.
Notes: Dec 2025 Whole of System (Core Crown) Report on Treaty Settlement Delivery shows 83.3% of settlement commitments complete or on track (up from 76.7% in 2024), with PSGE feedback included for the first time. Continuous honouring is underway but not complete.

Commitment: Remove co-governance from the delivery of public services.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Healthy Futures (Pae Ora) Amendment Act 2026 in force 10/07/2026 repeals s16A (engaging with and reporting to Māori) and amends Health NZ's duties to iwi-Māori partnership boards. Oranga Tamariki s7AA Treaty duties repealed, in force 08/04/2025; Māori Health Authority abolished 2024. Co-governance only partly unwound across public services, so held at 25.

Commitment: Restore the right to local referendum on the establishment or ongoing use of Māori wards, including requiring a referendum on any wards established without referendum at the next Local Body elections.
Stop all work on He Puapua
Confirm that the Coalition Government does not recognise the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) as having any binding legal effect on New Zealand.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: In its UPR response (Goldsmith release 27/09/2024) the Government noted but did not support eight recommendations to implement UNDRIP, saying indigenous rights are protected by existing legal and constitutional arrangements; RNZ/Te Ao Māori News reported the coalition position that UNDRIP has no binding legal effect. No standalone ministerial statement confirming non-binding status was found.

Commitment: Amend section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area Act to make clear Parliament’s original intent, in light of the judgment of the Court of Appeal in Whakatohea Kotahitanga Waka (Edwards) & Ors v Te Kahui and Whakatohea Maori Trust Board & Ors [2023] NZCA 504.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act 2025 (2025 No 58) received Royal Assent 24/10/2025 and came into force 25/10/2025. It amends section 58 to restore Parliament's original test for customary marine title, overriding the 2023 Court of Appeal Whakatōhea decision. Bill passed third reading in October 2025. Commitment delivered.

Commitment: Amend the Waitangi Tribunal legislation to refocus the scope, purpose, and nature of its inquiries back to the original intent of that legislation.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Te Ao Māori News (19/08/2026) reports the ITAG review findings are with ministers under active consideration; release undecided. TPK proactively released the review papers (page updated 28/07/2026), including the April 2025 Cabinet paper. Review announced 09/05/2025 (Bruce Gray KC chair). No Treaty of Waitangi Act amendment bill introduced.

Commitment: Conduct a comprehensive review of all legislation (except when it is related to, orsubstantive to, existing full and final Treaty settlements) that includes “The Principles ofthe Treaty of Waitangi” and replace all such references with specific words relating to therelevance and application of the Treaty, or repeal the references.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: MoJ page (updated 6 October 2026) says Cabinet on 14 September 2026 approved three omnibus bills for introduction (Standardisation; Strength of Legislative Obligations; Repeals Amendment Bills); introduction to Parliament not yet confirmed. Earlier: review completed; Cabinet on 23 February 2026 decided to amend 19 Acts (repeal seven references, specify two, cap ten at 'take into account'). Waitangi Tribunal urged a halt on 31 July 2026; government pressing ahead. Held at 40 until bills are introduced.

Commitment: The Government will not progress the development and delivery of National’s manifesto commitment to a “Taxpayer’s Receipt” for taxpayers.

National’s Going for Housing Growth policy will now accommodate the ACT/National agreement to make the Medium Density Residential Standards (MDRS) optional for councils, and to consider sharing a portion of GST collected on new residential builds with councils.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Budget 2026 (28/05/2026) allocated $400m over four years to the Incentives for Growth Fund (per-consent payments from April 2027) in place of a statutory GST share. Consenting Amendment Act (in force Aug 2025) lets only Auckland and Christchurch opt out of MDRS; HUD (16/10/2026) says MDRS will be replaced in Phase 3 RM reform. Law firm reports Planning and Natural Environment Bills passed third reading; Royal Assent not yet verified.

Commitment: The Parties confirm no ongoing commitment to income tax changes, including threshold adjustments, beyond those to be delivered in 2024.
Notes: Negative commitment honored: no further income tax threshold adjustments delivered beyond 2024 tax package across Budgets 2024, 2025 and 2026. Coalition pledge to refrain from further income tax changes appears to have been kept.

Commitment: Full cost benefit analysis must be presented before any binding agreement is made with respect to the Waikato medical school.
Notes: Initial action: Sign an MoU with Waikato University to progress a third medical school. Cabinet required a Detailed Business Case and full cost-benefit analysis (Sapere) before any binding agreement. The DBC identified Waikato as the preferred option (BCR 1.986); Cabinet approved the business case in July 2025 and the government confirmed it would proceed. Ground broken December 2025.

Commitment: National’s commitment to supercharge electric vehicle infrastructure with a comprehensive, nationwide network of 10,000 public EV chargers by 2030 will specifically take into account ACT’s concern that there be robust cost benefit analysis to ensure maximum benefit for government investment.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: CarExpert (23/03/2026) reports the Government announced $52.7m in zero-interest loans to ChargeNet and Meridian for 2,574 new public chargers. Bishop said NZ had just over 1,800 public charge points plus 161 in progress, taking the planned total to about 4,550 against the 10,000-by-2030 target. Rollout continues; no published cost-benefit analysis found.

Commitment: Legislate to improve the quality of regulation, ensuring that regulatory decisions are based on principles of good law-making and economic efficiency, by passing the Regulatory Standards Act as soon as practicable.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Regulatory Standards Act 2025 enacted 18/11/2025 and in force 01/01/2026; Part 2 requirements (consistency assessments against the principles of responsible regulation) in force 01/07/2026, per the Ministry for Regulation. The commitment to pass the Act is delivered.

Commitment: Immediately establish a new ministerial portfolio for Regulation.

Establish a new government department, required to assess the quality of new and existing legislation and regulation, funded by disestablishing the Productivity Commission and consolidating some regulatory quality work across the public sector where appropriate.
Notes: Ministry for Regulation established and operational (regulation.govt.nz); funded via Productivity Commission disestablishment. Department-level commitment delivered.

Commitment: In consultation with the relevant Minister, carry out regulation sector reviews, which could include the primary industries, the finance sector, early childhood education, and healthcare occupational licencing, in each case producing an omnibus bill for regulatory reform of laws affecting the sector.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Ministry for Regulation has completed sector reviews of hospitality (24 recommendations, Sept 2026, to a Hospitality Action Plan) and product labelling (Cabinet agreed a focused package), plus earlier agriculture/horticulture products and industrial hemp reviews; a building consent exemptions review began Oct 2026. RSAB omnibus-bill guidance issued Dec 2025. No omnibus reform bill found for any of the illustrative sectors (primary industries, finance, ECE, healthcare occupational licensing).

Commitment: Rewrite the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act 2003 to protect vulnerable consumers without unnecessarily limiting access to credit.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered with changes. Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Amendment Act 2026 in force 01/07/2026. It moves regulation to the FMA and eases 2019-era compliance (repeals the s 99(1A) cost-of-borrowing consequences, the director due-diligence duty and annual returns). Compromise: the 2003 Act was amended, not rewritten.

Commitment: Amend the Overseas Investment Act 2005 to limit ministerial decision making to national security concerns and make such decision making more timely.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Overseas Investment (National Interest Test and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2025 received Royal Assent 19/12/2025 and came into force 06/03/2026 by Order in Council. It adds a national interest test with a 15-working-day cap on initial risk assessments; the regulator must consent unless a transaction is referred to the Minister as contrary to the national interest (including national security and public order). The test is 'national interest', broader than the commitment's 'national security'. Initial 100-day action: policy decisions to ease build-to-rent investment.

Commitment: Reform market studies introduced by the Commerce Amendment Act 2018 to focus on reducing regulatory barriers to new entrants to drive competition.
Notes: Commerce (Promoting Competition and Other Matters) Amendment Bill (introduced Dec 2025) includes market-study tweaks; select committee (June 2026) removed a proposed standalone market-study power and clarified the Commission may recommend pro-competition regulation. No Royal Assent found by mid-August 2026. NZ Initiative argues the bill does not confine market studies to regulatory barriers.

Commitment: Deliver savings in public sector spending by reducing non-essential back office functions, with expenditure reduction targets to be set for each agency, informed by the increase in back office head count at that agency since 2017.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: On 19/05/2026 Willis announced the core public service will shrink from about 63,600 to about 55,000 staff by mid-2029 via mergers, further operating budget cuts and AI, framed against headcount growth since 2017. Budget 2024 delivered back-office savings across agencies (e.g. corporate services cuts at Police, FMA, Archives NZ). Per-agency targets explicitly tied to back-office growth since 2017 not confirmed, so 50.

Commitment: Restore mortgage interest deductibility for rental properties with a 60 per cent deduction in 2023/24, 80 per cent in 2024/25, and 100 per cent in 2025/26.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered with changes. IRD confirms landlords can claim 80% of residential interest for 2024/25 and 100% from 01/04/2025, so full deductibility is restored. Change: the backdated 60% deduction for 2023/24 was not implemented (Seymour: not worth the benefit).

Commitment: Repeal the Clean Car Discount.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Discount Scheme Repeal) Amendment Act 2023 received Royal assent 19/12/2023 and came into force 01/01/2024; the discount ended 31/12/2023.

Commitment: Narrow the Reserve Bank’s remit, to focus on price stability, and take advice on replacing “medium term” with specific time targets.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: RBNZ (Economic Objective) Amendment Act 2023 (in force 20/12/2023) made price stability the sole economic objective; the amended MPC Remit (13/12/2023) removed maximum sustainable employment and kept a 1-3% target over the medium term. No public record found of advice on replacing "medium term" with specific time targets.

Commitment: Amend the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021 to remove the dual mandate and take advice on removing the Treasury observer and returning to a single decision maker model
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Dual mandate removed by the RBNZ (Economic Objective) Amendment Act 2023 (assent 19/12/2023, in force 20/12/2023). No public record found of advice on removing the Treasury observer from the MPC or returning to a single decision-maker model.

Commitment: Repeal the Fair Pay Agreement regime by Christmas 2023.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Act 2023 received Royal assent 19/12/2023 and came into force the day after (20/12/2023), meeting the Christmas 2023 deadline.

Commitment: Reform health and safety law and regulations.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Health and Safety at Work Amendment Act 2026 received Royal assent 09/07/2026 and comes into force 01/04/2027, refocusing the regime on critical risks and amending the GRWM Regulations. Separate regulatory amendments (e.g. hazardous substances, recreation, laboratories) are in Cabinet, consultation or draft, so the regulations limb is not complete.

Commitment: Expand 90-day trials to apply to all businesses.

Consider simplifying personal grievances and in particular removing the eligibility for remedies if the employee is at fault, and setting an income threshold above which a personal grievance could not bepursued.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Employment Relations Amendment Act 2026 received Royal assent 20/02/2026 and came into force 21/02/2026. It removes or reduces remedies where the employee contributed to the grievance and bars unjustified-dismissal (and related disadvantage) claims for employees on new agreements earning $200,000 or more.

Commitment: Maintain the status quo that contractors who have explicitly signed up for a contracting arrangement can’t challenge their employment status in the Employment Court.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Employment Relations Amendment Act 2026 (assent 20/02/2026, in force 21/02/2026) excludes "specified contractors" from the meaning of employee: a worker meeting the written-agreement and independence criteria cannot recharacterise the arrangement in the Employment Court; otherwise the common-law test applies.

Commitment: Increase the cap on the number of workers under the Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme to increase the flexibility of the quota allocation system.
Notes: Cap increased from 19,500 to 20,750 for the 2024/25 season (announced 14 August 2024). RNZ (6 August 2026) confirms that level remains; Cabinet set aside a later proposal to scrap the cap entirely.

Commitment: Introduce a five year, renewable parent category visa, conditional on covering healthcare costs, with consideration of a public healthcare levy.
Notes: Parent Boost visa announced 10 June 2025; applications opened 29 September 2025. Multi-entry 5-year visa, renewable once (up to 10 years total). ACT's Parmjeet Parmar confirmed commitment fulfilled. Healthcare levy replaced with private health insurance requirement — substantive deviation from ACT's original proposal.

Commitment: Remove median wage requirements from Skilled Migrant Category visas.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered with changes. SMC changes took effect 24/08/2026 (INZ): new Skilled Work Experience (1.1x SMC median wage) and Trades and Technician (median wage) pathways, and no higher wage needed at residence stage. Compromise: median-wage tests were lowered and simplified, not removed; the existing pathway still uses 1.5x the median wage, and red/amber occupation lists restrict eligibility.

Commitment: Liberalise the rules to make it easier for family members of visa holders to work in New Zealand, beginning with Skilled Migrant Category visa holders.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: INZ Amendment Circular 2026-09 (effective 20/04/2026) clarifies open work visa holders, including partners, may be self-employed, and lets partners of Business Investor and Entrepreneur work visa holders do any work. Earlier, open work rights were restored from 2/12/2024 for partners of AEWV holders in ANZSCO 1-3 roles and some lower-skilled roles. First step (skilled-migrant families) delivered; wider family-member liberalisation remains incremental.

Commitment: Amend the Resource Management Act 1991 to make it easier to consent new infrastructure including: renewable energy, allow farmers to farm, get more houses built, and enable aquaculture and otherprimary industries.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Several RMA amendment Acts are in force: Freshwater and Other Matters (Oct 2024), Consenting and Other System Changes (in force Aug 2025), and Duration of Consents (in force 17/12/2025). Resource Management (Auckland Housing) Amendment Act in force 3/4/2026. The RMA itself is now being replaced by the Planning Act 2026 and Natural Environment Act 2026 (assent 30/09/2026).

Commitment: Replace the Resource Management Act 1991 with new resource management laws premised on the enjoyment of property rights as a guiding principle.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Planning Act 2026 and Natural Environment Act 2026 received Royal assent 30/09/2026 after third readings on 22/09/2026 (RNZ). Most provisions commence the day after assent, but repeal of the RMA and other parts commence by Order in Council (any part not in force within 4 years commences then). New system expected fully operational 2029-2030. Bills were reported back 20/07/2026 and passed second reading 4/08/2026.

Commitment: Institute long-term city and regional infrastructure deals, allowing PPPs, tolling and value capture rating to fund infrastructure.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Three City and Regional Deals signed: Auckland (10/04/2026), Western Bay of Plenty (14/05/2026) and Otago Central Lakes (06/10/2026) (MCERT). Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Act 2026 (in force 5/08/2026) broadens the value-capture levy tool. Deals do not devolve powers; whether deals themselves use PPPs or tolling is not yet evident.

Commitment: Introduce financial incentives for councils to enable more housing, including considering sharing a portion of GST collected on new residential builds with councils.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Delivered with changes. Budget 2026 (28/05/2026) allocated $400m over four years to the Incentives for Growth Fund, paying councils a tiered share of national average consent value for each new home consented. GST-sharing was considered but not adopted; the fund is the chosen incentive. Compromise: first payments are not made until 01/04/2027.

Commitment: Legislate to make the MDRS optional for councils, with the need for councils to ratify any use of MDRS, including existing zones.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Resource Management (Auckland Housing) Amendment Act 2026 (in force 3/04/2026) governs Auckland Council's withdrawal of MDRS rules from Plan Change 78 via Plan Change 120. The 2025 Consenting Act gave only Auckland and Christchurch MDRS opt-outs. Bishop said in June 2025 MDRS would not be made optional for other councils; remaining MDRS settings to be replaced under the new planning system.

Commitment: Remove the Kāinga Ora Sustaining Tenancies Framework and ensure appropriate consequences for tenants who engage in repeated antisocial behaviour.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Ministers ordered Kāinga Ora to end the Sustaining Tenancies Framework in March 2024; a new disruptive behaviour policy allowing faster termination followed (RNZ, 14/07/2024: 14 terminations in three months vs 8 in all of 2023). Later: 553 Section 55A warnings July-Dec 2024 (RNZ, 10/01/2025); 63 tenancies terminated by 1 June 2025 per the Associate Housing Minister.

Commitment: Explore allowing home builders to opt out of needing a building consent provided they have long-term insurance for the building work.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Building Amendment Bill (introduced 29/06/2026, at select committee) requires home warranties for residential work of $100,000+ and professional indemnity insurance for designers, with an Order in Council power to disapply them. It has no general building consent opt-out for insured builders. The 18/08/2025 consent reform announcement said Cabinet was investigating home warranties (with an opt-out) alongside proportionate liability. Related consumer protection, not the opt-out itself.

Commitment: Work to replace fuel excise taxes with electronic road user charging for all vehicles, starting with electric vehicles.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Scored as delivered on review (19/10/2026). Light electric vehicles moved onto road user charges from 01/04/2024; the wider switch from fuel excise to RUC for other light vehicles is still being legislated.

Commitment: Work with Auckland Council to implement time of use road charging to reduce congestion and improve travel time reliability.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Auckland Council's transport committee shortlisted three time-of-use charging options on 25/08/2026 (city centre, city fringe, central motorways), with public engagement from November 2026 and a final council decision targeted for early 2028, then ministerial approval. The enabling Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Act 2025 received assent 18/11/2025 and comes into force 18/11/2026. No Auckland scheme operating yet.

Commitment: Reverse speed limit reductions where it is safe to do so.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Setting of Speed Limits Rule 2024 (in force 30/10/2024) required speed limits cut since 2020 on specified road classes to be reversed by 01/07/2025. NZTA reports state highway reversals implemented by 01/07/2025. After consultation, 6 urban connector sections kept lower limits and 43 returned to higher limits, consistent with 'where it is safe'.

Commitment: Allow landlords to issue a 90 day notice to a tenant to end a periodic tenancy without providing a reason or applying to the Tenancy Tribunal.
Return tenants’ notice period to 21 days and landlords’ to 42 if the tenant wished to move or landlord wished to sell a property.
Introduce “pet bonds” to make it easier for tenants to have pets in rental properties.

Maintain a split-gas approach to methane and carbon dioxide through to 2050 and review the methane science and targets in 2024 for consistency with no additional warming from agricultural methane emissions.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The Climate Change Response (2050 Target and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2025 (in force 17/12/2025) keeps a separate biogenic methane target, resetting it from 24–47% to 14–24% below 2017 levels by 2050, and requires a further target review by 2040. This followed the 2024 independent methane science review and the Government's 12/10/2025 announcement, which also ruled out agricultural methane pricing. Commitment met.

Commitment: Reform the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee to ensure its functions, membership and mandate are appropriate.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: NAWAC's 2025 annual report (approved April 2026) says its code-of-conduct guideline remains on hold awaiting 'proposed reform of NAWAC's function, membership and mandate', so the reform is not done. June 2024 ministerial expectations letter directed NAWAC to weigh practicality and cost, engage stakeholders and reprioritise codes (a 'first step'). The Oct 2025 pig-code override is not a reform of NAWAC.

Commitment: Cease implementation of new Significant Natural Areas and seek advice on the operation of existing Significant Natural Areas as part of the Government’s programme to reform the Resource Management Act.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: RMA section 78, inserted by the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2024 and in force 25/10/2024, suspends the NPSIB requirements to identify and notify new SNAs for 3 years (to 25/10/2027) while SNAs are reviewed as part of RMA replacement.

Commitment: Improve Farm Environment Plans so they are more cost-effective and pragmatic for farmers.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: On 19/08/2026 ministers announced risk-based freshwater farm plan decisions: certification and audit only for higher-risk activities (via an amendment paper to the Natural Environment Bill), lighter mapping and reporting, pass/fail audits, 6-year recertification and 5 years to comply. Regulations are still to be drafted. The 2025 Amendment Act already raised the threshold to 50 ha (exempting about 8,000 farms) and allowed industry certification.

Commitment: Enable farmers and landowners to offset sequestration against their on-farm emissions.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: The second emissions reduction plan (published 17/12/2024, amended January 2026), chapter 12, commits to a framework to recognise non-forest removals, including on-farm riparian plantings and shelterbelts, in the ETS or another mechanism. Assessment criteria are 'progressing', with no recognition yet. On-farm agricultural emissions pricing by 2030 has been dropped. The earlier 33 rested on pre-coalition ETS forestry rules.

Commitment: Replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 to allow district councils more flexibility in how they meet environmental limits and seek advice on how to exempt councils from obligations under the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 as soon aspracticable.
Notes: As at 19/10/2026: Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2024 (in force 25/10/2024) removed the NPS-FM hierarchy of obligations from consenting while the NPS-FM is reviewed and replaced, barred councils from notifying freshwater plans before a replacement NPS-FM or 31/12/2025, and created a ministerial exemption pathway. No replacement NPS-FM confirmed as published. 50 = exemption/flexibility limb delivered; replacement limb outstanding.

Commitment: Update the Crown Minerals Act 1991 to clarify its role as promoting the use of Crown minerals.
